extracted.intended_audience: students/readers of elementary algebra and arithmetic (historical Italian mathematical text)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory rules and procedures for forming and manipulating squares, binomials, and products using geometric (area) interpretations and algebraic decomposition — i.e., how to represent products as surfaces, expand squares of sums, and distribute multiplications. This is an excerpt from a historical Italian arithmetic/algebra treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product as surface (area) representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent numbers as line segments and their product as the area (superficie) of the rectangle determined by those segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute products by interpreting them geometrically: divide the rectangle into component parts (squares and rectangles) corresponding to parts of the factors; the whole rectangle's area equals the sum of those component areas. Use this partition to convert multiplicative problems into sums of simpler rectangular/square areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square of a binomial (expansion rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The square of a binomial equals the square of the first term plus twice the product of the two terms plus the square of the second term (quadrato del binomio = quadrato del primo + doppio prodotto + quadrato del secondo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you form (a + b)^2, decompose the corresponding square-surface into the square on a, the square on b, and the two equal rectangles each of area a·b; sum these three contributions to obtain the full square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive multiplication of sums (multiply each part by each part)
rubrics_metrics.description: To multiply sums (or binomials/multinomials), multiply every part of one sum by every part of the other and add the resulting partial products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly form the partial rectangles/surfaces for each pair of terms (e.g., for (a+b)(c+d) form ac, ad, bc, bd) and sum them. The treatise repeatedly recommends partitioning quantities and performing multiplication term-by-term, then combining like parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute by partitioning numbers into convenient parts
rubrics_metrics.description: When numbers are large or not perfect squares, decompose them into smaller parts (units, tens, other convenient sub-quantities), multiply the parts pairwise, and recombine the partial products to obtain the overall product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises reducing a compound multiplication to operations on parts to make calculation manageable: reduce many factors to a single fold by successive multiplications of parts, and keep track of the partitioning so partial areas correspond to correct positional values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of doubles and quadruples in relation to squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate doubling/quadrupling of quantities to squares and products: e.g., the double (or quadruple) of a certain area/product corresponds to predictable combinations of squares and cross-products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise explains identities connecting twice a product, quadruple of a number, and squares (for instance, quadruple relations arise from doubling processes and from comparing squares of doubled quantities). Use these relations to simplify or check computations (e.g., comparing the square of a sum with sums of squares and double products).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling non-square (irregular) numbers via decomposition and complement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a number is not a perfect square, handle it by expressing it as sum/difference of square parts and remaining parts (complements) so that geometric/square methods still apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text demonstrates that by splitting a non-square quantity into a square part plus remainder (or by pairing with other terms), one can still form rectangle/square decompositions and apply the expansion or distributive rules to compute or reason about the quantity.
